description: Watch ops — spawn background pollers for external sources (MRs, jobs, calendar) that emit events via UDS socket + status files + macOS notifications. Reusable foundation; channel consumer plugs in later.

watch.description: Spawn a background poller for SOURCE:ID. Optional :only=ev1,ev2 filters which events emit notifications. PID file: /tmp/supertool-watch-{SOURCE}__{ID}.pid

unwatch.description: Stop every live poller for SOURCE:ID and remove its PID file. A slot can hold more than one poller, so this is a multi-kill: the tracked PID plus any poller whose own argv names this exact source and id. Every PID is printed with its provenance (tracked/untracked) before anything is signalled, one that cannot be stopped is named rather than swallowed (exit 1), and an absence is only reported as an absence when the process scan actually ran — 'no PID file', 'tracked PID is dead', and 'could not check' are three different answers. A poller spawned before the argv labelling landed wears its parent's command line and cannot be reached; those need `pkill -f presets/watch/` once.

watches.description: List active watch pollers as a table: source, id, pid, started, last_event. Built from PID files AND a scan for labelled poller processes, so it also shows what the PID files alone cannot: an id running more than one poller (count plus every PID), and a poller whose PID file was deleted ('no pidfile'). This is the authoritative view of the fleet — `ps` output cannot identify a watcher, because a poller spawned before the argv labelling wears the argv of whatever forked it.

channel.description: Whether the watch -> Claude-session bridge is actually delivering (#554). `pgrep channel.ts`, `lsof` on the socket and writing to it are all green whether events arrive or not, so this asks a different question and answers it in five states, never two. NOT DELIVERING (exit 1) is a definite negative — nothing is listening, so every event a poller emits right now is lost at the source, and the report names the watchers that already were. FORWARDING (exit 0) reads the consumer's own published counters: lines read, forwarded, dropped, last forwarded, refreshed on a 10s heartbeat so an idle consumer and a wedged one are distinguishable. CANNOT DETERMINE (exit 3) is everything else — bound but publishing no counters, counters written by a pid that is gone, counters gone stale — and it is the state today's tooling reports as green. It now names the process holding the socket, so `nothing is consuming this` and `another session is consuming this` stop rendering identically: `socket-holder: pid N — not this process`, or the refusal the probe returned, never a bare verdict. CONTRADICTED (exit 4) is separate from it because a contradiction is not an absence of findings: the health file was written by a process that is not the one holding the socket. BOUND, NOT SUBSCRIBED (exit 5) is the state #1543 was filed for — a consumer bound, verified and counting, with NO session subscribed to its channel, so every event it reads is handed on and discarded. Subscription is only partly observable from outside the target session and this claims exactly the part that is: the process that spawned the socket-holder, and whether the channel tag in its argv (`--dangerously-load-development-channels server:NAME`) names an MCP server the harness has configured, asked with `claude mcp get` — the same question the oss plugin's bin/oss-workspace asks before it registers the consumer. No tag, an unconfigured tag (which is what a `--mcp-config` server produces) and a session that has exited are definite negatives; no `ps`, no `claude` on PATH or an argv that does not parse is CANNOT DETERMINE **with the reason**, never FORWARDING. That probe costs a `claude` invocation, ~1-3s measured 2026-08-13, which is why this op is no longer instant and why it is classed `acts` rather than `read-only`: `claude mcp get` health-checks by spawning the named server, the name comes out of another process's argv, and so a blind probe of this op starts whatever the harness has configured under it (#1558). Every lookup in one run shares a 12s budget so the probe always fits inside this op's timeout — a probe that cannot answer before its own op times out can never reach `CANNOT DETERMINE`, and the reader gets a bare `TIMEOUT` with an empty body instead. A tag the budget did not reach is named as unasked, never as unconfigured. The tag is shape-checked and passed after `--` (#1559): only shapes no server name can have are excluded (empty, leading `-`, control chars). The connect status the lookup prints is deliberately NOT read: it spawns a second instance, and this repo's consumer refuses to start a second one (#550), so `Failed to connect` is what a healthy singleton reports. `forwarded` means handed to the MCP transport and never means delivered: the bridge sends a JSON-RPC notification, which has no response to wait on, so whether an event reached a session is observable only from inside that session. Honours SUPERTOOL_WATCH_NAME, which derives both the socket and the poller state directory from one word; SUPERTOOL_WATCH_SOCK and SUPERTOOL_WATCH_STATE_DIR still override it and the report prints the override. Nothing in .supertool.json reaches the consumer: the harness spawns it, so the name reaches it by environment export, which is what the oss plugin's bin/oss-workspace does (#1541 — an `env` block in the shipped .mcp.json would write one checkout's private name into an artifact every user installs). This op reads that file anyway and reports a disagreement, or says the consumer inherits an environment nobody here can read, rather than assuming agreement. Branch on the report's first line (`channel: FORWARDING|NOT DELIVERING|CANNOT DETERMINE|CONTRADICTED|BOUND, NOT SUBSCRIBED`) rather than on the exit code: the distinct codes 0/1/3/4/5 survive only when presets/watch/channel.py is run directly, because the supertool wrapper collapses every non-zero to 1. `channel:probe` is the other sub-op and the other question (#1593): health reports on traffic that already happened, and a consumer that is bound, verified and counting publishes the same numbers whether it is reading its socket or wedged on it, so with no traffic of its own nothing says whether the path works RIGHT NOW. probe writes one synthetic event with a reserved source (`channel-probe`), impersonating no watcher and writing no watcher state file, then re-reads the consumer's published counters for up to 3s and reports which one moved: FORWARDED (exit 0) when `forwarded` advanced; ACCEPTED, DISCARDED (exit 7) when `dropped` did instead — the burst budget or a routing key over the attribute cap, and the consumer's own stderr names which; ACCEPTED, NOT FORWARDED (exit 6) when `lines_read` moved and neither of the others did, which is a finding about the read loop; NOT DELIVERING (exit 1) when nothing took the bytes; CONTRADICTED (exit 4) when the counters were published by a process that is not the one holding the socket; and CANNOT DETERMINE (exit 3) for everything it could not measure — no baseline, an unreadable re-read, no `lines_read` to separate `has not read it yet` from `read it and handed it nowhere`, or a consumer that simply had not read the line inside the wait. It never renders `forwarded` as arrival: the bridge sends a JSON-RPC notification with no response to wait on, so the last leg is observable only from inside the receiving session. What it does instead is name the exact tag the caller should now look for — `<channel watcher_source="channel-probe" id="probe-XXXXXXXX" event="probe">`, with a per-run id so a stale tag on screen cannot answer for a fresh probe — and state that an advance is not attributable either, because a poller emitting in the same window advances the same counter. `channel:received:N` is the third sub-op (#2150, #2051 remedy 1) -- a session's own count of events received, against `forwarded`'s advance since the last report: AGREE, DISAGREE by N, or UNSETTLED (never AGREE) when no window can be diffed. See docs/presets/watch.md.

radar.description: Reconcile registered radar tiers against live truth, then report. Tiers are registered in ops.radar.radar_tiers (as SUPERTOOL_RADAR_TIERS) and there is no default: with none configured radar refuses and names the fix, because an unconfigured radar that prints nothing is byte-identical to a healthy one. `{"gl-mrs": {}}` is the GitLab MR board — live MRs are authoritative, state files are cache; it prunes terminal state files, flags pipeline drift (last_event vs source_state), respawns watchers for open MRs with no live poller, and keeps one gitlab-mr-feed poller alive so MRs opened after this run are still discovered. `{"gl-runners": {}}` adds the runner fleet. Full board on cold start, delta-only after. Idempotent — safe on every session start. Takes the gl-mrs filter vocabulary; the board, the watcher fleet and the feed are always one resolved filter. Standing exclusions live in ops.radar.radar_exclusions. {'gh-prs': {}} is the GitHub PR board — same reconcile, one `gh pr list` call, plus a standing gh-branch poller for the default branch, the red-master case no PR covers (#2024). It refuses a filter token it cannot honour instead of running the query without it, counts a PR with no check rollup as unchecked rather than green, keys its delta on the head SHA, and reports watch coverage as UNKNOWN under a repo target because watch state is keyed by PR number alone. Also spawns and heals a github-pr-feed poller (#1780); footer names each poller's state. `radar:--state` is the read-only view: which module each registered name resolved to, the options it accepted, the ones it did not recognise, and — for a tier exposing radar_state() — its resolved scope, snapshot file and live pollers. It spawns nothing, reaps nothing and calls no API, so it is safe when you only want to look, while a bare radar heals and forks pollers. It is an argument rather than its own op because ops.radar.radar_tiers merges into the op it is keyed by, so a second op name would need a second copy of the tier list — and a read-only view describing a different tier set from the one radar runs is the very defect it exists to remove.
